title: The Association of Self-Compassion and Social Anxiety with Assessment and Workload Stress in Australian University Students
content: University students who experience high levels of stress during their studies are likely to have less course satisfaction and a lower depth of learning. In this study we explored self-compassion and social anxiety as potential determinants of assessment and workload stress in Australian university students.  A total of 1,006 students (517 men & 480 women) from a range of aca-demic disciplines completed a survey containing the variables of interest. As expected, for both forms of stress, self-compassion was associated with lower levels of stress and social anxiety was associated with higher levels of stress. Social anxiety also partially mediated the effect of self-compassion, and all effects were evident controlling for age. Exploratory analyses showed no gender differences in the patterns of findings for assessment stress. For workload stress, however, the partial mediation effect in male participants was confined to social interaction anxiety, whereas, for female participants, mediation was determined by social performance anxiety. Additionally, women scored higher than men on workload stress and social performance anxiety and lower than men on self-compassion.  Our findings suggest that interventions which increase self-compassion and reduce social anxiety are likely to relieve assessment and workload stress in higher education students and thus improve their engagement with study.
